artifacts.title: Online Prescribing Service Intake Questionnaire Summary
artifacts.author: Online Women's Health Service
artifacts.body: Patient-completed online intake for combined hormonal contraception. Reported: no history of blood clots, no smoking (per questionnaire response 'No'), no migraines reported, BP 'unknown/not checked - patient self-attested normal'. Questionnaire did not include a specific question distinguishing migraine with vs. without aura. Service approved prescription based on self-reported answers without a live visit or BP measurement.

artifacts.title: Pharmacist Interaction & Contraindication Screen
artifacts.author: Pharmacy clinical decision support system
artifacts.body: ALERT 1 (Contraindication - Major): Combined hormonal contraceptive + migraine with aura -> increased risk of ischemic stroke. Classified as Category 4 (unacceptable health risk) under the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) for this specific indication; the UK MEC and US MEC (CDC) similarly classify migraine with aura as Category 4 for combined hormonal contraceptives, though these national adaptations are not identical to WHO MEC across all conditions (for example, postpartum VTE risk categories differ) and should not be assumed interchangeable in general. ALERT 2 (Drug-Herb Interaction - Moderate): St John's wort (Hypericum perforatum) induces CYP3A4 and may reduce serum levels and efficacy of ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel, increasing risk of breakthrough bleeding and contraceptive failure. ALERT 3 (Missing Data): No blood pressure documented within past 12 months; baseline BP required before initiating combined hormonal contraceptive per clinical guidelines.

artifacts.title: Pharmacist Counseling / MTM Note - Draft
artifacts.author: Pharmacy student (community rotation), co-signed by supervising pharmacist
artifacts.body: Patient presented to collect new prescription for combined oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol 30 mcg/levonorgestrel 150 mcg) intended for contraception and hoped benefit for acne. History-taking revealed monthly migraines preceded by visual zigzag aura and ~20 minutes of right-hand tingling, consistent with migraine with aura - a contraindication to estrogen-containing contraceptives due to stroke risk. No blood pressure documented within the past 12 months. Patient also taking St John's wort (unlisted supplement) which may reduce contraceptive efficacy, and reports occasional nicotine vaping. Dispensing withheld; prescriber contacted to discuss alternative (progestin-only or non-hormonal) method and need for BP measurement. Patient counseled on interim contraception/barrier method pending resolution and on acne skincare options not requiring systemic hormonal therapy.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient initially states she does not smoke or vape at all.
mismatches.recordEvidence: After direct, nonjudgmental follow-up (action a9), patient discloses weekend nicotine vaping started about a year ago; this is documented in the counseling note as an unlisted substance use relevant to overall cardiovascular risk assessment alongside the contraceptive decision.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may underreport nicotine/vaping use, especially framing it as 'not really smoking.' Direct, nonjudgmental follow-up questions are needed, and disclosed nicotine use should be documented and factored into cardiovascular risk counseling even though vaping alone is not an absolute CHC contraindication the way aura is.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes her blood pressure 'has always been fine' and doesn't think a check is urgent.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Vital Signs History flowsheet (d3) shows the only BP on file is from 2 years ago (118/74 mmHg); nothing has been measured since, including today.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patient reassurance based on old or absent data is not a substitute for a current measurement; combined hormonal contraceptive initiation requires a documented baseline BP, and online prescribing without this step is a gap in care the pharmacist should catch.

objectives.text: Elicit a focused headache history sufficient to identify migraine with aura (visual and sensory aura preceding headache) as a major contraindication to combined hormonal contraceptives.

Recognize that absence of a documented blood pressure within the past 12 months is a required screening gap before dispensing combined hormonal contraception, and distinguish patient reassurance from objective data.

Identify a clinically significant drug-herb interaction (St John's wort reducing combined oral contraceptive efficacy) through careful, nonjudgmental medication/supplement reconciliation, including supplements the patient may not consider 'medications.'
Use nonjudgmental, direct follow-up questioning to uncover socially sensitive information (nicotine vaping) initially denied by the patient, and document its relevance to overall counseling.

Correctly manage a prescription with a major contraindication by withholding dispensing and contacting the prescriber to discuss alternatives, rather than counseling and dispensing as requested or independently changing the prescription, staying within pharmacy scope of practice.
Address the patient's acne concern with accurate, scope-appropriate information, noting that this specific contraceptive is not being dispensed today and that non-hormonal acne care options exist.

answerKey.primaryProblem: New online-prescribed combined oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel) with a major undetected contraindication (migraine with aura) and additional gaps: no baseline blood pressure, undisclosed interacting supplement (St John's wort), and undisclosed nicotine vaping - requiring the pharmacist to withhold dispensing and contact the prescriber rather than counsel-and-dispense.
differential: Appropriate candidate for combined hormonal contraceptive pending further screening (ruled out once aura confirmed)
Migraine without aura with incidental hand paresthesia unrelated to headache (less likely given consistent 20-minute prodrome preceding each headache)
Tension-type headache mislabeled as migraine (unlikely given classic aura description and existing neurology diagnosis)
keyFindings: Monthly headaches preceded by visual zigzag aura and ~20 minutes of right-hand tingling - migraine with aura
No blood pressure documented in the past 12 months; last BP 118/74 mmHg was 2 years ago
Online prescribing service questionnaire did not ask about aura and approved the prescription on self-reported, unverified answers
Unlisted St John's wort use (2-3 times/week) not previously in pharmacy profile, a CYP3A4 inducer that can reduce contraceptive efficacy
Nicotine vaping on weekends, initially denied, disclosed only after direct follow-up
Mild-moderate inflammatory acne along jawline/chin, currently managed only with OTC benzoyl peroxide wash
plan: Do not dispense the ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel prescription today; document the clinical concern in the pharmacy record

Contact the prescribing telehealth service to report migraine with aura and absent baseline BP, and request an alternative method (e.g., progestin-only pill, non-hormonal method) or appropriate workup before any estrogen-containing product is dispensed
Advise patient to use condoms (already her current method) or discuss other non-hormonal/progestin-only contraception with a prescriber in the interim

Counsel patient that combined hormonal contraceptives are not an appropriate source of acne treatment in her case given the aura finding, and discuss non-hormonal acne care (consistent OTC benzoyl peroxide or salicylic acid use, referral to primary care or dermatology if OTC measures are insufficient)

Counsel on the interaction between St John's wort and hormonal contraceptives generally, and advise discussing her low mood and supplement use with her primary care provider for safer, evidence-based options
Provide brief, nonjudgmental counseling on nicotine vaping as a cardiovascular risk factor relevant to future hormonal contraceptive decisions, and offer cessation resources if patient is interested
Flag the chart for pharmacist follow-up once the prescriber responds; do not independently substitute or modify the prescription
Document all findings and communications clearly in the pharmacist counseling/MTM note
redFlags: Migraine with aura + estrogen-containing contraceptive = increased risk of ischemic stroke (absolute contraindication)
No baseline blood pressure before initiating combined hormonal contraception
Prescribing based solely on an online questionnaire without validated screening for aura or BP measurement
educationPoints: Migraine with aura (visual and/or sensory symptoms preceding headache) is a WHO/CDC Category 4 contraindication to combined hormonal contraceptives due to stroke risk; migraine without aura is not an absolute contraindication at this age.

Direct-to-consumer online prescribing questionnaires may miss key screening questions (such as distinguishing aura from non-aura migraine) and may not require objective measurements like blood pressure.

Patients often do not consider herbal supplements like St John's wort to be 'medications' and may not volunteer them unless specifically asked; St John's wort is a potent CYP3A4 inducer that can reduce hormonal contraceptive efficacy and increase breakthrough bleeding/pregnancy risk.
Patients may underreport nicotine or vaping use initially; nonjudgmental, direct follow-up questions improve disclosure.

When a prescription has a major safety contraindication discovered at counseling, the pharmacist's role is to withhold dispensing and communicate with the prescriber about alternatives - not to independently approve, deny, or substitute therapy outside their scope.

Combined hormonal contraceptives are sometimes effective for acne, but this benefit does not outweigh a major contraindication such as migraine with aura; non-hormonal acne care options should be discussed.

scenario.studentBrief: You are a pharmacy student on a community pharmacy rotation, supervised remotely by a pharmacist, conducting a telehealth video visit. Chloe Bennett, 22, is calling to pick up (via mail/curbside coordination) a new prescription for a combined oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol 30 mcg/levonorgestrel 150 mcg) sent by an online telehealth prescriber. She also fills sumatriptan for migraines through your pharmacy. Conduct new-prescription counseling: confirm indication and understanding, screen for contraindications, interactions, and adherence barriers, and decide whether it is appropriate to dispense today.

profile.title: New Online-Prescribed Combined Oral Contraceptive with Undetected Migraine Aura
profile.summary: A 22-year-old university student arrives for a telehealth pharmacy visit to collect a first-time combined oral contraceptive prescribed by an online telehealth service, also hoping it will help her acne. Through careful history-taking the student must uncover migraine with aura, missing baseline blood pressure, an undisclosed interacting supplement (St John's wort), and initially-denied nicotine vaping, then correctly withhold dispensing and escalate to the prescriber rather than counsel-and-dispense. The case teaches contraindication screening, medication/supplement reconciliation, nonjudgmental disclosure elicitation, and appropriate scope-of-practice escalation in community pharmacy.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in her off-campus bedroom in Bristol, Connecticut, connecting from her phone before heading to class
